text: Lesson four introduced rail-optimized topology at a glance. This lesson goes deeper into how a fabric like solara-train's is actually built out of switches.

The basic shape is a fat-tree, also called leaf-spine. Leaf switches connect directly to groups of compute nodes. Spine switches connect the leaf switches to each other. No two nodes ever talk directly — traffic between nodes on different leaf switches always goes leaf, to spine, to leaf, no matter how far apart those two nodes physically sit in the data center.

The number that actually matters for collective performance is bisection bandwidth — split the cluster into two halves, the worst possible way, and ask how much data can move between those halves at once. For something like ring AllReduce, where data genuinely has to cross between every pair of nodes, that ceiling is what determines how fast the whole cluster can actually communicate.

That's where oversubscription comes in. If a leaf switch has more downlink capacity to nodes than uplink capacity to the spine — say sixteen nodes at four hundred gigabits feeding into only eight times four hundred gigabits of uplink — that's two to one oversubscribed. Fine for traffic that rarely needs full cross-leaf bandwidth at once. Wrong for collective-heavy training, where many nodes often do need that bandwidth simultaneously — which is why training fabrics are built non-blocking, one to one, instead.

Fat-tree for the overall shape, non-blocking for bisection bandwidth, rail-optimized layered on top for how GPU-indexed traffic moves across it — that's what a well-designed training fabric looks like, and it's exactly how solara-train's 64 nodes are wired. Up next, lesson eleven, closing out the chapter: diagnosing a bottleneck when the topology doesn't deliver what it promised.
